Estimate a population total from a sample

Source: R/variance.R
ht_total.Rd

Forms the Horvitz-Thompson total sum(y / pi) with a standard error, a confidence interval and a design effect, using a variance estimator matched to how the design actually randomised.

Usage

ht_total(
  sample,
  y,
  variance = c("auto", "analytic", "jackknife", "none"),
  level = 0.95,
  by = NULL,
  df = NULL,
  alternative = c("two.sided", "less", "greater"),
  contrast = NULL,
  ratio = NULL
)

Arguments

sample

A data frame returned by draw() with weights = TRUE. See "Which columns are read".

y

The variable to total: a column name, several column names, a numeric vector as long as sample, or a single number, which stands for that value in every row. A factor or character column, or a factor as long as sample, gives the count of each level. See "Several variables" and "Categories".

variance

How to compute it. "auto" uses the design's own estimator (see "Variance") and falls back to the jackknife when that declines; "analytic" insists on the design's own estimator, returning NA with the reason in note rather than falling back; "jackknife" uses the jackknife, and returns NA with the reason in note for systematic and Poisson samples, where it does not apply; "none" skips it. The result reports which was used in method, and "none" when nothing could produce a figure.

level

Confidence level for the interval.

by

Optional column name(s) in sample defining domains. When given, the result is one row per domain. See "Domains". A column named like one of the table's own, such as n or se, is refused.

df

Degrees of freedom for the interval. NULL uses the design's (see "Confidence intervals"); Inf gives a normal interval; otherwise a single number of 1 or more.

alternative

"two.sided" for a confidence interval, "less" for a one-sided upper bound or "greater" for a lower bound, each at level. See "Confidence intervals".

contrast

Optional weights over the by domains, as a named numeric vector such as c(a = 1, b = -1) for domain a less domain b. A name is the domain's value of a single by column, or the values of several joined by " . ", as in "a . east", the way the notes of a by table name domains. Needs by. See "Contrasts".

ratio

Optional name of a numeric column x of the frame, for the ratio estimator of the total, sum(y / pi) / sum(x / pi) times the frame's total of x. Not with by. See "Ratio estimation".

Value

A list with a print() method, holding:

total

The Horvitz-Thompson total, sum(y / pi).

variance, se, ci, level, alternative, df

Its estimated variance, standard error, confidence interval or one-sided bound, and the degrees of freedom the interval used. NA where the design supports no variance.

ci_scale

The scale the interval was formed on: "linear" for a total, and "logit" or "beta" for a proportion from ht_mean().

variable

The name of y when it is a column name, and NULL when it is a vector.

n, n_random, design

Rows used, those of them not taken with certainty, which the beta interval of a proportion counts as its sample size, and the design's type.

deff

The design effect — see deff().

method

Which estimator produced the variance. See "Variance".

note

Why a variance is missing, what approximation was used, or which fallback was taken. NULL when an exact estimator applied cleanly.

unreachable

Rows of the frame with inclusion probability 0, which the estimate does not cover; NA for a sample saved by drawn 0.2.0. See "Rows the design cannot reach".

unavailable

For a sample from use_reserves() only, the number of those rows found unavailable. The estimate takes every frame row nobody visited as available; see "What the estimates describe" in use_reserves().

With ratio, the list also holds ratio, the estimated ratio of y to x, x, the column's name, and frame_total, its total over the frame.

With by, a data frame of class drawn_by instead: one row per domain, with the domain columns, n (an integer), total, variance, se, ci_lower, ci_upper and method, and the level, alternative, scale, degrees of freedom, notes, unreachable count and variable as attributes. It prints without variance, which is the square of se. A by table has no design effect.

With contrast, a list of class drawn_contrast with a print() method, holding contrast, the weighted sum; weights and estimates, the weight and estimate of each domain it weighs; what ("total" or "mean"), estimator for a mean, and by; and variable, variance, se, ci, level, alternative, df, n, n_random, ci_scale, design, method, note and unreachable as above. deff is NA.

With several column names as y, a drawn_by table with a row for each variable, or each variable and domain, led by a variable column; see "Several variables". With a factor or character y, the same table with a row for each level, led by a level column; see "Categories".

Each has coef(), vcov(), confint(), as.data.frame() and tidy() methods; see "Working with the result".

Variance

Each design gets the estimator the survey-sampling literature recommends for it, and method in the result says which one was used:

"analytic"

Exact and design-unbiased. Fixed-size designs with known joint probabilities use the Sen-Yates-Grundy estimator. For simple random, reservoir and spatial samples, strata and intervals it reduces to the textbook formula built from the variance of y within each stratum or interval, and for an equal-take design_multistage() to the two-stage formula built from the variance between the estimated cluster totals and within clusters (Särndal, Swensson and Wretman 1992). Those formulas are what is computed, in time and memory that grow with the number of sampled rows rather than with its square. Poisson sampling, whose rows are independent, uses sum((1 - pi) / pi^2 * y^2); cluster designs apply the estimator at the cluster level, because taking whole clusters makes the row count random; certainty designs hand the problem to rest, since certainty rows are in every sample and add nothing. A design_systematic() sample with n_starts of 2 or more uses the variance between its replicates' totals, the random group estimator (Wolter 2007), on n_starts - 1 degrees of freedom.

"deville"

Systematic probability-proportional-to-size (design_weighted() with method = "systematic"). Its joint probabilities have no closed form, so this uses Deville's (1999) approximation, which needs only the first-order probabilities and is the best-performing of the standard approximations for high-entropy designs (Matei and Tillé 2005). Randomised systematic selection is close to high entropy (Hartley and Rao 1962). Unlike a plain jackknife, each row's contribution is scaled by its own 1 - pi, so rows near certainty stop adding variance they do not have. With strata it is added up over the strata. design_multistage() with size applies it to the estimated totals of the clusters, and adds the variance within them.

"successive difference"

design_systematic(). The design has one random start, and at a step of 2 rows or more neighbouring rows are never drawn together, so no design-unbiased estimator exists. This uses the successive-difference approximation, which compares each sampled row with its neighbour in the order the design walked (Wolter 2007), at every step, including a step under 2 rows, where every pair of rows can be drawn together. It removes a trend along that order rather than counting it as noise, which is why it beats treating the sample as simple random: on a frame sorted by a variable related to y, the simple random formula overstated the variance two- to thirtyfold in the package's simulations. This one came closer, but its average over the random starts depends on the frame, and on the estimation article's example it was 1.6 times the true variance. No estimator from a single systematic sample escapes its limits. A frame that cycles with a period equal to the step, or one that divides it, such as 5 rows at a step of 10, puts every row of one sample at the same phase of the cycle, and the variance is understated, to under 0.001 of the truth in one simulation. A period of twice the step puts neighbouring sampled rows at opposite phases, and the variance is overstated, 29-fold in the same simulation. When a smooth trend so dominates y that the random start is almost the only source of variation, it runs low, and has no floor. It was 0.3 to 0.7 of the truth when the trend spanned 25 noise standard deviations, 0.2 at 100 and 0.06 at 1,000. With y a straight line along the walk and no noise, it is 6 * k / (n * (k + 1)) times the truth, about 6 / n, for n rows sampled at a step of k. When interval does not divide the number of rows walked, the sample size is random, one of two values, and the total moves with it in a way successive differences cannot see. A term for that, mean(y / pi)^2 * (r / k) * (1 - r / k) with k the interval and r the remainder, is added, and the note says so. Without it a constant y had a standard error of 0, and a variable with a coefficient of variation of 0.02 an interval that never covered the truth. A design given n draws exactly n rows at a step of N / n and needs no such term. design_stratified() with within = design_systematic() adds up this estimator over its strata.

"local mean"

design_spread(). A spatially balanced sample is well spread precisely because neighbours are rarely taken together, so this compares each sampled row with the local mean of its nearest sampled neighbours (Stevens and Olsen 2003; Grafström and Schelin 2014). With strata it runs within each stratum, and the strata's variances are added.

"jackknife"

The delete-one-unit jackknife, by stratum (JKn) where the design has strata, and deleting whole clusters where it has them. Used when requested, and as the fallback under variance = "auto".

Rows taken with certainty are in every possible sample and add nothing to the variance. That covers rows above a design_certainty() threshold, rows whose size puts them past certainty in design_weighted() or design_spread(), strata taken whole, clusters taken whole by a two-stage design that selects every cluster, and a census. Every estimator leaves them out. The jackknife holds them fixed instead of deleting them, and its finite population correction counts only the other units. A sample made of nothing else has a variance of 0 under the design's own estimator.

The analytic estimator declines — returning NA with the reason in note — rather than understate. Only a decline sends variance = "auto" to the jackknife. Any other error inside an estimator, such as running out of memory, stops ht_total() with that error. Two cases matter in practice:

  • A stratum or interval with a single sampled row. There is no variation inside it to measure, and simply leaving it out, as the Sen-Yates-Grundy sum does, reports a standard error that is too small — zero, if every stratum is like that. Draw at least two per stratum (min_per_stratum = 2, per_interval = 2).

  • One row per cluster in a multistage design. Two rows of one cluster are never drawn together, so the within-cluster variation is unmeasurable. With f1 = n_clusters / N_clusters, the share of clusters selected, the exact estimator understates by f1 times the within-cluster component of the variance. variance = "auto" falls back to the delete-a-cluster jackknife, the ultimate-cluster approximation standard in survey practice. It has no first-stage finite population correction, so it overstates by f1 times the between-cluster component, the variance the cluster totals would have if clusters were drawn with replacement. The excess is small when few clusters are selected. With 30 of 40 clusters whose totals differed widely, the jackknife averaged 3.3 times the true variance. Whenever f1 is above 0.2, the note gives the factor by which the jackknife inflates the between-cluster part. When every cluster is selected, the clusters are strata and the variance between them is zero by design, so design_stratified() with the cluster column as strata and two rows in each gives an exact variance instead.

A Sen-Yates-Grundy estimate that comes out negative is treated the same way: a failure of the estimator on an unlucky sample, not a variance.

Confidence intervals

Intervals use Student's t with the design's degrees of freedom — the number of primary sampling units minus the number of strata — rather than the normal distribution (Korn and Graubard 1999). The difference is negligible with hundreds of units and decisive with a handful: at four clusters a normal interval covers about 87% where it claims 95%, and the t interval restores most of that. The degrees of freedom used are reported as df; pass df = Inf for the normal interval.

Units taken with certainty count in neither number. They are in every sample and carry no variance, and counting them made the interval too narrow. With eight certain units among ten, systematic PPS reported 9 degrees of freedom where the variance rests on two units, and its interval covered 79%. A stratum or interval with no other unit drops out of the count of strata. With no unit below certainty the variance is 0 and df is Inf. as_svydesign() hands certain units to survey in a form that makes survey::degf() give the same count, except for a census, where it gives n - 1.

An estimate whose variance is 0 is exact and gets a zero-width interval whatever df is. Otherwise a design that leaves 0 degrees of freedom, such as Poisson sampling that drew one row, gives a standard error but no interval, and note says why. df set by hand must be at least 1. A proportion of 0 or 1 is the exception to the first rule; see "Proportions" in ht_mean().

The t interval assumes the estimate is close to normally distributed over repeated samples. When y / pi is skewed and the sample small it is not, and the interval covers less often than level says, even where the variance estimate is close to unbiased. In 2,000 draws with n = 30 from 240 rows in proportion to a size whose coefficient of variation was 0.66, with y close to proportional to size, the 95% interval for the total covered 90% of the time under systematic PPS and 94% under Poisson PPS. The mean with estimator = "ht", which ht_mean() recommends in that case, is the total divided by N and covered as often. The default Hajek mean covered 91% under both methods. Skew is one reason. The Hajek mean also has a ratio bias, here 1.5% of the mean under systematic PPS and 1.8% under Poisson PPS, and its estimated variance averaged 0.89 and 0.88 times the variance of the mean over the draws. Skew lowers coverage under equal probabilities too. A simple random sample of 30 from 600 lognormal values with a coefficient of variation of 1.5 covered 87%. A larger sample brings the coverage closer to level. The audit-sampling article checks a bound's coverage by drawing the design many times, which is how to check it on a frame of your own.

alternative = "less" gives a one-sided upper bound, the figure an auditor signs off against, and "greater" a lower bound. The other end of ci is then -Inf or Inf, or 0 or 1 for a proportion, and the printout labels the bound. A one-sided bound at level is the end of a two-sided interval at 1 - 2 * (1 - level), so the 95% upper bound is the upper end of the 90% interval, which level = 0.90 also gives.

Rows the design cannot reach

Rows with inclusion probability 0, such as rows past max_items, outside a region or time window, dropped by na_rm or in a stratum allocated no rows, can never be drawn, so a total covers the other rows only. draw() warns about some of them by name. The estimate keeps their number in unreachable and prints it on a line of its own, since a sample saved and read back, or drawn with the warning muffled, would otherwise give no sign of them. The design effect is measured against a simple random sample of the rows the design can reach; see deff().

An empty sample

A design of random size, such as Poisson sampling or a systematic sample whose random start falls past the last row, can draw nothing. ht_total() then returns a total of 0, which keeps the estimator unbiased over repeated draws, with df 0, the variance, standard error and interval NA, and a note that the sample is empty. ht_mean() refuses the Hajek mean of an empty sample, which is 0 / 0; estimator = "ht" gives 0. An empty sample from a design that gives every row a probability of 0, such as one with n = 0, is refused, and so is any empty sample in as_svydesign().

Domains

by estimates for each level of one or more columns — sites, regions, months — without subsetting the sample first. Subsetting a sample and treating the piece as its own sample gets the variance wrong, because the number of rows that happen to fall in a domain is itself random. Here each domain's total is estimated from y * (row in domain) over the whole sample, so the same design and the same variance machinery apply (Särndal, Swensson and Wretman 1992, section 10.3).

Domains come out in key order: a factor's levels, numbers and dates in sequence, and text sorted byte by byte as in the C locale, the same in every session. A domain with no sampled row is left out, as survey::svyby() leaves it out.

A stratum or interval with a single sampled row stops a domain's variance, as it stops the whole sample's, unless it holds no unit of the domain. That is read from the by columns of the frame stored with the sample, so it needs them in the frame, with the same values as in the sample. A domain made of strata taken whole is then exact, with a zero-width interval. A lonely stratum whose one sampled row lies outside the domain still stops it when other units of the stratum belong to the domain, because their variation went unmeasured. A frame row whose by value is missing may belong to any domain, so a lonely stratum holding one stops every domain.

A domain's Hajek mean (ht_mean()) needs sampled rows in at least two primary sampling units, rows or clusters. Its linearised residuals sum to zero inside the unit that holds the whole domain, so with one unit every estimator gives a standard error of about 0, and survey does the same. Such a domain gets no standard error, with a note. When stage one of a cluster design takes every cluster, the analytic estimator's units are rows, since each cluster is then in every sample and only its rows were drawn at random. The jackknife still deletes whole clusters, so a domain inside one cluster gets no standard error from it, whether variance = "jackknife" asks for it or "auto" turns to it after the analytic estimator declines. Rows taken with certainty count as one unit, since every estimator holds them fixed and as_svydesign() hands them to survey together, so a domain whose sampled rows were all taken with certainty gets no standard error either, unless every row of it that the design could reach is certain, which makes its mean exact. A domain total, and the estimator = "ht" mean, keep the standard error of 0 their estimators give such a domain, since those estimators are unbiased over samples, and a note says the interval has no width because the sampled rows were all certain. A domain with a handful of sampled rows has a standard error that is itself unreliable, and the interval covers less often than level says. In one simulation of a skewed variable, a 95% interval for the mean of a domain with two or three sampled rows covered 65% of the time, and 85% with four or five.

A sample grouped with dplyr::group_by() is estimated as a whole, with a warning of class drawn_grouped_df; the groups play no part. Use by.

The strata, clusters and other pieces the variance reads from the frame are worked out once for all the domains. For simple random, reservoir, spatial, stratified and temporal samples the analytic variances of all the domains come from one pass over the sample, in time that grows with the number of sampled rows rather than with rows times domains. A domain with units in a stratum or interval of one sampled row, and every domain under variance = "jackknife", is estimated on its own.

Contrasts

contrast weighs the domain estimates of by and gives their weighted sum, such as the difference between two sites' totals or means, with a standard error, an interval and df as for any other estimate. Each domain's estimate is the total, over the whole sample, of a variable that is 0 outside the domain: y for a total, the linearised residual for a Hajek mean and y / N_d for a Horvitz-Thompson mean. The weighted sum of the estimates is the total of the same weighted sum of those variables, so one run of the design's variance estimator gives its variance, with the covariances between domains included. For simple random, stratified, cluster and multistage samples the standard error equals that of survey::svycontrast() applied to survey::svyby(..., covmat = TRUE).

The interval is symmetric, for a proportion too, since a difference of proportions can be negative. Domains left out of contrast have a weight of 0. A name that is not a domain with a sampled row is refused, and so is a contrast whose weights are all 0. When a Hajek mean that the contrast weighs rests on one primary sampling unit, the contrast gets no standard error, for the reason given under "Domains".

Ratio estimation

ratio names a column x of the frame, and the total of y is then estimated by the ratio estimator sum(y / pi) / sum(x / pi) * X, where X is the total of x over the frame rows the design can reach, read from the frame stored with the sample, as frame_totals() reads it. When y is close to proportional to x, such as an audited value and the book value it was drawn on, the residuals y - R x vary far less than y, and the estimate is more precise than the Horvitz-Thompson total. Its variance is X^2 times that of the ratio from ht_ratio(), estimated from the residuals X (y - R x) / X_hat with the design's own estimator, and it equals predict(survey::svyratio(~y, ~x, design), total = X) for the designs as_svydesign() maps with identical standard errors. The sampled rows' values of x come from the frame too. A value of x missing from a frame row the design can reach is refused, since X is then unknown, and so is ratio with by. The result holds the ratio as ratio, the column as x and X as frame_total, and prints them.

The ratio estimator is biased, by an amount of order 1 / n, and its design effect compares it with the same estimator from a simple random sample of the same size. Calibration in survey, with the totals from frame_totals(), covers several auxiliary columns at once.

Several variables

y may name several columns, such as c("spend", "visits"). The result is then a drawn_by table with a row for each variable, or for each variable and domain with by, led by a variable column. Each row holds what a call for that variable alone gives: the same estimate, standard error, interval and method, with the same refusals for a missing or infinite value, named by its column. Notes that hold for every variable are printed once, and the others after the variable's name.

vcov() of the table gives the covariances between the variables' estimates as well as their variances. Every variance estimator here is a quadratic form in the variable it totals, so the covariance of two estimates whose variables are z_a and z_b is (V(z_a + z_b) - V(z_a) - V(z_b)) / 2, one more run of the same estimator. For a total these variables are the y columns, and for a Hajek mean their linearised residuals. For the designs as_svydesign() maps with identical standard errors, the matrix equals vcov(survey::svytotal(~a + b, design)), or that of survey::svymean() for means. With by, the covariances between the variables within each domain are estimated, and those between domains are not, as for a by table of one variable. A covariance is NA when either variance is missing, or when the two variances, or the variance of their sum, did not come from one estimator, as when the design's own declined for one and the jackknife stood in.

A by column named variable is refused, and so is contrast. The table has no design effect.

Categories

A factor or character column named as y, or a factor as long as sample, is split into a 0/1 indicator for each of its levels: ht_total() gives the estimated number of frame rows at each level, and ht_mean() the share of each, with a proportion's interval. The result is the table of "Several variables" with a row for each level, or each level and domain with by, led by a level column in place of variable, and vcov() holds the covariances between levels. The levels are a factor's levels, unused ones included, and the values of a character column sorted byte by byte. A missing value is a missing y. For the designs as_svydesign() maps with identical standard errors, the estimates and vcov() equal those of survey::svytotal(~f, design) and survey::svymean(~f, design). A character vector given as y is read as column names, so pass categories held in a vector as a factor. A by column named level is refused, and so is contrast; the indicator of one level, such as sample$f == "a", takes it.

A single number as y stands for that value in every row: ht_total(sample, 1) estimates the number of frame rows the design can reach, and with by the number in each domain.

Working with the result

coef() gives the estimate, named after y when y is a column name, vcov() its variance as a 1 by 1 matrix, and confint() its interval as a matrix with a column for each end. At the estimate's own level, confint() returns the interval the estimate holds. At another level it forms the interval again on the design's degrees of freedom and on the estimate's scale (ci_scale), so it gives what level = in ht_total() or ht_mean() would have given. survey::SE() and survey::cv() work through coef() and vcov().

as.data.frame() gives one row of variable, n, the estimate, variance, se, ci_lower, ci_upper, level, df, deff and method, so estimates of several variables can be bound with rbind(). With the generics package installed, generics::tidy(), and so broom::tidy(), gives term, estimate and std.error, with conf.low and conf.high when conf.int = TRUE, at conf.level, which is the estimate's own level unless given.

A by table has the same methods. coef() names each domain as contrast names it, confint() and tidy() give a row per domain, tidy() with the by columns, and as.data.frame() drops the table's class and attributes. vcov() holds the domains' variances. The covariances between domains are not estimated, and its entries for them are NA, except 0 for two domains of a design_stratified() sample whose sampled rows share no stratum, since strata are sampled independently. The standard error of a difference between domains comes from contrast, not from vcov(). A table of several variables names each row by its variable, then its domain, as in "spend . a", and its vcov() holds the covariances between variables described under "Several variables". Selecting columns of the table with [ or subset() drops the attributes these methods read, and the result prints as a plain data frame. Selecting rows keeps them. A drawn_contrast has the same methods, with the estimate named by its weights, as in "a - b", and so does a ratio from ht_ratio(), named as "y/x".

Missing values and nonresponse

ht_total() refuses a missing y, from a nonresponse or a measurement that failed. A total over the rows with y present counts the others as 0, so it is low by about the share of the weight they hold, the weighted nonresponse rate, and the message gives that share.

ht_mean(na_rm = TRUE) estimates the mean over the rows with y present. They are a domain of the whole sample, as a by domain is: the estimate is the Hajek mean over them, and its variance comes from the linearised residuals over every sampled row, 0 for the rows left out, with the design's own estimator and degrees of freedom. survey::svymean(na.rm = TRUE) on as_svydesign() gives the same estimate and standard error. With by, each domain's mean is over its rows with y present, and a domain whose sampled rows all have y missing has no mean, no row in the table and no place in contrast; the note names it. add_fieldwork() joins results keyed by an id and leaves y missing for a sampled row with none.

That mean is unbiased for the frame's mean only if the values are missing completely at random, with no relation between whether a row has a y and its y. When response rates differ between groups whose y differs, such as sites, the rows with y present over-represent the groups that responded more. A weighting-class adjustment corrects for that, under the weaker assumption that response is unrelated to y within each group. Multiply the .weight of each row with y present by its group's sum of .weight over all its sampled rows, divided by the same sum over its rows with y present, and estimate totals and means from as_svydesign() with survey's na.rm = TRUE. survey treats the adjusted weights as fixed, so its standard errors leave out that the adjustment factors were estimated from the sample. ht_total() and ht_mean() keep to .prob and do not see the adjustment. The estimation article shows the steps.

A unit that cannot be reached at all, rather than one that does not answer, can be replaced from a reserve list drawn with the sample: reserve in design_simple() and design_spread(), then use_reserves(). The estimates then describe the units that can be reached.

Which columns are read

ht_total() and ht_mean() divide by .prob, the inclusion probabilities draw() attached, find each sampled row's frame row through .row, and read strata, clusters, time stamps and the other design columns from the copy of the frame stored with the sample. Of the sample's own columns they read .prob, .row, y and by, and .weight only to warn when it was edited, so renaming, recoding or dropping a design column in the sample changes nothing.

.weight is not used in the estimate. A weight adjusted after the draw, for nonresponse or by trimming, and written into .weight is ignored with a warning of class drawn_weight_edited; as_svydesign() hands .weight to survey, which is where adjusted weights are estimated from. A sample whose .prob was changed or removed is refused. So is one whose design gives the frame different inclusion probabilities in the current session than it did at draw time, which a change of sf::sf_use_s2() does to a design_spatial() sample: the variance is recomputed from the design and would describe another one. A sample saved by drawn 0.2.0 has no .row and records no probabilities for the frame, so its rows are matched by position and it is refused when the design gives a sampled row a probability other than its .prob.

References

Horvitz, D. G. and Thompson, D. J. (1952). A generalization of sampling without replacement from a finite universe. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 47, 663–685. doi:10.1080/01621459.1952.10483446

Sen, A. R. (1953). On the estimate of the variance in sampling with varying probabilities. Journal of the Indian Society of Agricultural Statistics, 5, 119–127.

Yates, F. and Grundy, P. M. (1953). Selection without replacement from within strata with probability proportional to size. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B, 15, 253–261. doi:10.1111/j.2517-6161.1953.tb00140.x

Hartley, H. O. and Rao, J. N. K. (1962). Sampling with unequal probabilities and without replacement. Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 33, 350–374. doi:10.1214/aoms/1177704564

Deville, J.-C. (1999). Variance estimation for complex statistics and estimators: linearization and residual techniques. Survey Methodology, 25, 193–203.

Matei, A. and Tillé, Y. (2005). Evaluation of variance approximations and estimators in maximum entropy sampling with unequal probability and fixed sample size. Journal of Official Statistics, 21, 543–570.

Wolter, K. M. (2007). Introduction to Variance Estimation, 2nd ed. Springer. doi:10.1007/978-0-387-35099-8

Korn, E. L. and Graubard, B. I. (1999). Analysis of Health Surveys. Wiley. doi:10.1002/9781118032619

Särndal, C.-E., Swensson, B. and Wretman, J. (1992). Model Assisted Survey Sampling. Springer. doi:10.1007/978-1-4612-4378-6

Examples

set.seed(1)
pop <- data.frame(
  id = 1:200,
  site = rep(c("a", "b"), times = c(150, 50)),
  spend = round(stats::runif(200, 10, 500))
)

s <- draw(pop, design_stratified("site", n = 40), seed = 1, weights = TRUE)
ht_total(s, "spend")
#> Horvitz-Thompson total  (stratified design, n = 40)
#>   estimate 54,000
#>   se       3,713.698  (analytic)
#>   95% CI  46,482.01 to 61,517.99  (t, 38 df)
#>   deff     1.03  (about the same as simple random sampling)

sum(pop$spend)   # the truth
#> [1] 52732

# One estimate per site, from the same sample
ht_total(s, "spend", by = "site")
#> Horvitz-Thompson total by domain  (stratified design, 95% CI, t, 38 df)
#>  site  n total   se ci_lower ci_upper   method
#>     a 30 40715 3152    34334    47096 analytic
#>     b 10 13285 1963     9310    17260 analytic
tapply(pop$spend, pop$site, sum)
#>     a     b 
#> 39123 13609 

# How much more site a spent than site b
ht_total(s, "spend", by = "site", contrast = c(a = 1, b = -1))
#> Contrast of Horvitz-Thompson totals  (stratified design, n = 40)
#>   contrast `a` - `b`
#>   domains  `a` 40,715, `b` 13,285
#>   estimate 27,430
#>   se       3,713.698  (analytic)
#>   95% CI  19,912.01 to 34,947.99  (t, 38 df)

# Two variables at once, with the covariance between their totals
s$visits <- round(s$spend / 50) + 1
both <- ht_total(s, c("spend", "visits"))
both
#> Horvitz-Thompson total by variable  (stratified design, 95% CI, t, 38 df)
#>  variable  n total     se ci_lower ci_upper   method
#>     spend 40 54000 3713.7    46482    61518 analytic
#>    visits 40  1285   75.1     1133     1437 analytic
vcov(both)
#>             spend    visits
#> spend  13791552.3 277139.69
#> visits   277139.7   5640.23
